header: Muhammad Fazil & others Vs Muhammad and others.
Mr. Abdul Sattar Khan, Advocates, for petitioners.
M/s Mian Hikmatullah Jan, Saifur Rehman, Shahid
Mushtaq and Nazeer Ahmad, Advocates, for
body: MUHAMMAD NAEEM ANWAR, J.- Muhammad Fazil and two others have sought review of the judgment dated 11.09.2026 rendered in Writ Petition No. 6788-P/2025, whereby the application filed by respondent No.1 under Order XXI Rule 29, read with Section 151 CPC, was allowed to the limited extent of staying execution of the decree insofar as it related to the property known as Jabir Plates, until final adjudication of Suit No. 62/1 of 2011. The learned Executing Court was, however, directed to proceed with execution of the decree in respect of the remaining subject matter, to the extent executable in accordance with law, while refraining from executing the same insofar as it pertained to Jabir Plates until final decision of the aforesaid suit.

2. Mr. Abdul Sattar Khan, learned counsel for the applicants, contended that the omission of Rule 29 of Order XXI CPC and the subsequent insertion of Rule 29-A had not been brought to the notice of this Court at the time of deciding the writ petition. According to him, the former provision no longer formed part of the statute, whereas the latter was confined to suits arising out of proceedings under Rule 63 of Order XXI CPC, which provision had also ceased to form part of the statute. He, therefore, maintained that the judgment sought to be reviewed proceeded on a statutory provision which was no longer in force. In support of his contention, he placed reliance upon the judgments reported as Yaqeen Shah v. Haji Pir Sher Bacha and another (PLD 1964 West Pakistan 57) and Tarak Nath Sen v. Kartick Chandra Sen and another (PLD 1960 Dacca 786). He added that an application under the relevant provision of law was maintainable only in the suit and not in the execution proceedings. According to him no suit was pending adjudication before the learned Civil Court and that the scope of Rule 29 could not be extended to proceedings relating to an appeal arising out of a suit that had already been dismissed. Lastly, he submitted that possession of the property had already been delivered to the decree-holder; however, following the decision of the writ petition through the judgment now sought to be reviewed, the respondents, who are the plaintiffs in the connected suit, instituted proceedings under Section 144 CPC, seeking restitution of possession of the property. According to learned counsel, the subsequent proceedings themselves demonstrated the erroneous exercise of jurisdiction by this Court.

3. Mr. Nazeer Ahmad, Advocate, learned counsel for respondent No.5, adopted the arguments advanced by learned counsel for the applicants. He additionally submitted that an application filed by the plaintiffs of the pending suit under Section 151 CPC, read with all other enabling provisions of law, had been brought on record through C.M. No. 102-P/2026. He further apprised the Court that possession of the property had already been delivered to the decree-holder on 26.09.2025, as was evident from the statement of the decree-holder recorded before the learned Executing Court. He accordingly maintained that the subsequent claim for restitution was not legally sustainable.

4. Conversely, Mr. Hikmatullah Jan, Advocate, learned counsel representing respondent No.1, supported the judgment sought to be reviewed. He submitted that the application seeking suspension of execution proceedings had been dismissed by the learned Executing Court on 04.06.2025, which order was subsequently challenged through W.P. No. 6788-P/2025. He emphasized that, on the date of dismissal of the application, possession of the disputed property was still with the respondents/plaintiffs of the connected suit and that its delivery to the decree-holder on 26.09.2025 took place subsequently. Learned counsel further referred to the order dated 20.05.2014 passed by the learned Senior Civil Judge, whereby it had been directed that possession of Jabir Plates would remain subject to the final decision of the civil suit. He submitted that the said direction was reiterated through a subsequent order dated 15.01.2025 passed by the learned Senior Civil Judge in Suit No. 212/1 of 2014. According to him, delivery of physical possession to the decree-holder was in disregard of the aforesaid judicial directions, which had attained finality and had never been challenged by the present applicants. He, therefore, contended that the subsequent delivery of possession could neither defeat the subsisting judicial directions nor render the claim of the respondents for protection of their rights infructuous. On these premises, he maintained that the review application was devoid of merit and liable to be dismissed.
5. Arguments heard; record perused.

6. Before addressing the objections raised in the review application, it would be appropriate to briefly delineate the factual background giving rise to the controversy. It is an admitted position that Muhammad Fazil and four others (respondent No.1 and his co-plaintiffs) instituted a suit in the year 2012, seeking recovery of possession through partition in respect of the properties described in Heads A to H of the plaint. Under Head G thereof, they specifically sought recovery of possession of their respective shares in the property known as Jabir Plates, which constitutes the subject matter of the application giving rise to the present controversy. Apart from the aforesaid suit, certain other suits, titled Muhammad Javed Khan and others v. Muhammad Ismail Khan and others and Muhammad Ismail Khan and others v. Muhammad Javed Khan and others, were also instituted between the parties. In Suit No. 362/1, a preliminary decree was passed, whereas Suits No. 62/1 and 61/1 were dismissed through judgment dated 20.05.2014. The controversy presently before this Court emanates from an application filed by respondent No.1 before the learned Senior Civil Judge, where execution proceedings arising out of the suit titled Muhammad Fazil and others v. Muhammad Javed Khan and others were pending. The applicant therein asserted that he was in possession of Jabir Plates Nos.1, 6, 10 to 12 and 19, a claim which, according to him, was also substantiated by the report of the Local Commission. He further maintained that, in view of the judicial directions dated 20.05.2014 and 15.01.2025, execution of the decree, insofar as it related to Jabir Plates, was required to remain subject to the final adjudication of the proceedings pending between the parties concerning the same property. Accordingly, he sought suspension of execution to that limited extent until final decision of the connected suit. The application was dismissed by the learned Courts below. However, this Court, through the judgment now sought to be reviewed, allowed the writ petition to the limited extent indicated hereinabove. It is against that judgment that the present review application has been instituted.

7. The first objection requiring consideration is that Rule 29 of Order XXI CPC had ceased to form part of the statute and, consequently, the judgment under review proceeded on a non-existent provision of law. The contention, on examination, is misconceived. A perusal of the relevant statutory provisions reveals that Rule 29 of Order XXI CPC continues to form part of the Code of Civil Procedure applicable to the present case. The omission of the said provision, upon which learned counsel for the applicants has placed reliance, was brought about through an amendment applicable to the Province of Punjab, notified in the Punjab Gazette dated 22.08.2018, bearing No. 237/Legis/XI-Y-26. The said provincial amendment cannot be extended to the Province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, nor can it be treated as having altered the statutory position governing the controversy in hand. The subsequent insertion of Rule 29-A, therefore, does not, by itself, establish that Rule 29 stood omitted from the Code applicable to the present proceedings. Both provisions have their distinct fields of operation and cannot be treated as interchangeable. For a proper appreciation of the distinction, the relevant provisions are reproduced below:

Order XXI Rule 29 CPC "29. Stay of execution pending suit between decree-holder and judgmentdebtor. Where a suit is pending in any Court against the holder of a decree of such Court, on the part of the person against whom the decree was passed, the Court may, on such terms as to security or otherwise, as it thinks fit stay execution of the decree until the pending suit has been decided." Order XXI Rule 29-A CPC "29-A. When a suit under Rule 63 of this Order is pending, the Court in which such suit is filed may if it considers that execution of the former decree should be stayed, intimate the fact to the executing Court, which shall thereupon stay execution until the suit is decided."

The distinction between the two provisions is apparent. Rule 29 deals with the power of the Court to stay execution of a decree where a suit is pending against the decree-holder at the instance of the judgmentdebtor. Rule 29-A, on the other hand, contemplates a distinct situation arising out of a suit instituted under Rule 63 of Order XXI CPC and provides for communication of the decision to stay execution to the Executing Court. The applicability of one provision cannot, therefore, be defeated merely by referring to the other.

8. Learned counsel for the applicants also placed reliance upon the judgment reported as Yaqeen Shah v. Haji Pir Sher Bacha and another (PLD 1964 West Pakistan 57). However, a perusal of the said judgment reveals that the controversy therein primarily concerned the interpretation and applicability of Rule 29-A of Order XXI CPC, whereas the matter presently under consideration relates to the scope and applicability of Rule 29 thereof. The ratio of the said judgment, therefore, does not govern the controversy in hand. Likewise, the judgment reported as Tarak Nath Sen v. Kartick Chandra Sen and another (PLD 1960 Dacca 786) does not advance the case of the applicants, as the controversy therein pertained to the interpretation of Order XXIX CPC and the expression "until the pending suit has been decided", which appears in Rule 29-A of Order XXI CPC. The said judgment does not lay down any principle that would render Rule 29 inapplicable to the circumstances obtaining in the present case. Consequently, neither of the judgments relied upon by learned counsel establishes that Rule 29 of Order XXI CPC was unavailable to the parties or that this Court exercised jurisdiction under a provision which had ceased to exist.

9. The next objection pertains to the status of the connected suit and the contention that, on the date of institution of the application under Order XXI Rule 29 CPC before the learned Executing Court, no suit was pending adjudication. It is an admitted position that, by that time, the suit instituted by respondent No.1 had been dismissed by the learned trial Court in exercise of its powers under Order XVII Rule 3 CPC, whereas an appeal against the order of dismissal was pending before the learned Appellate Court. It is equally significant that, before the application under Order XXI Rule 29 CPC came to be decided, the learned Appellate Court had already allowed the appeal, set aside the order dismissing the suit and restored it to its original position. Consequently, on the date of adjudication of the application, the suit stood restored and was pending adjudication before the competent Court. It is a well-settled principle of law that an appeal is a continuation of the original proceedings. The appellate proceedings do not constitute an independent lis divorced from the suit out of which they arise; rather, they form an integral continuation of the original proceedings for examining the legality and correctness of the order under challenge. Thus, the dismissal of the suit, having been challenged before the learned Appellate Court, had not attained finality. More importantly, the appellate proceedings culminated in setting aside the order of dismissal and restoring the suit to its original position before the application under Order XXI Rule 29 CPC came to be decided. In these circumstances, although the suit had ceased to remain pending before the learned trial Court on the date of institution of the application, the proceedings arising therefrom remained sub judice before the appellate forum. Upon acceptance of the appeal, the order of dismissal stood set aside and the suit was revived for adjudication on its merits. The legal effect of such restoration was that the suit regained its status as a pending proceeding, and its pendency could not be disregarded merely because it had temporarily stood dismissed before the trial Court. The material consideration, therefore, was the status of the suit when the application came up for adjudication, rather than its status merely on the date of its institution. Since the order dismissing the suit had, by then, been set aside and the suit restored to its original position, the statutory requirement of pendency of the suit stood fulfilled at the relevant stage. The objection raised by learned counsel for the applicants, therefore, proceeds on an incomplete appreciation of the procedural history of the connected litigation and does not disclose any error apparent on the face of the record warranting interference in review jurisdiction.

10. The contention that an application under Order XXI Rule 29 CPC could only be filed in the pending suit and not in the execution proceedings is also misconceived. The very object of the provision is to empower the Court to regulate execution of a decree where a suit involving the decree-holder and the judgment-debtor is pending before it. The provision expressly contemplates the exercise of jurisdiction in relation to execution proceedings and authorizes the Court to stay execution, subject to such terms as to security or otherwise as it considers appropriate. The jurisdiction conferred by Rule 29 is, therefore, ancillary to the execution proceedings and is intended to prevent an unjust or potentially conflicting exercise of the Court's authority where the rights of the parties are already the subject matter of another pending adjudication. The fact that the application is moved in the execution proceedings, rather than separately in the connected suit, does not render it incompetent. Indeed, it is the Executing Court which is required to consider whether, in the circumstances contemplated by the provision, execution should be stayed and, if so, to what extent. It must, however, be emphasized that the existence of jurisdiction under Rule 29 does not confer an unfettered or automatic right to obtain stay of execution. The use of the expression “may” in the provision signifies that the power conferred upon the Court is discretionary and must be exercised judiciously, in the light of the facts and circumstances of each case. Mere pendency of a suit between the decree-holder and the judgment-debtor does not, in itself, furnish sufficient ground for staying execution of the decree. The underlying principle is that a decreeholder is ordinarily entitled to enjoy the fruits of the decree and should not be deprived thereof merely because the judgment-debtor has instituted another proceeding. The power under Rule 29 is, therefore, to be exercised with circumspection and only where the circumstances of the case furnish sufficient justification for such interference. The Court must examine whether the subject matter of the pending suit substantially overlaps with the subject matter of execution, whether the outcome of the suit is likely to affect the rights sought to be enforced through execution and whether continuation of execution may occasion prejudice or result in conflicting adjudications. Any order of stay must also be proportionate to the controversy pending adjudication and should not unnecessarily obstruct execution of the decree in respect of matters not involved in the pending suit.

11. In addition, the circumstances were not those of an ordinary application seeking suspension of execution merely on account of pendency of another suit. The decree itself, read in the light of the relevant judicial directions, contained a qualification with regard to execution of the decree insofar as it related to Jabir Plates. The subject matter of the pending suit and the property sought to be excluded from execution were identical, at least to the extent of Jabir Plates. The rights claimed by the parties in respect of that property were already under adjudication, and the judicial directions dated 20.05.2014 and 15.01.2025 specifically required the matter to remain subject to the outcome of the connected proceedings. It was precisely this distinguishing feature which warranted a limited protection against execution in respect of Jabir Plates. This Court, while deciding the writ petition, did not suspend execution of the entire decree or deprive the decree-holder of its fruits in respect of the remaining properties. Rather, the direction was confined to the particular property whose rights were directly involved in the pending adjudication. The learned Executing Court, while declining the application, failed to give due effect to this material aspect of the controversy. The approach adopted by this Court was, therefore, not founded merely upon the existence of a pending suit but upon the combined effect of the identity of the subject matter, the subsisting judicial directions and the qualification governing execution in respect of Jabir Plates. These were the circumstances which justified the limited exercise of discretion under Order XXI Rule 29 CPC.

12. At this stage, it would be appropriate to examine the objection advanced by Mr. Nazeer Ahmad, Advocate, regarding delivery of possession of the property to the decree-holder on 26.09.2025 and the subsequent proceedings initiated by the respondents under Section 144 CPC. The objection requires consideration in the context of the doctrine of restitution and the legal effect of the subsequent events upon the rights of the parties. Section 144 CPC embodies the well-established principle of restitution, founded upon the maxim that an act of the Court shall prejudice no one. The underlying obligation of the Court is to ensure that no party suffers an injury or derives an unjust benefit as a consequence of an order or decree which is subsequently varied, reversed, set aside or modified. Where, as a result of such judicial determination, a party has received a benefit to which it is ultimately found not to be entitled, the Court is empowered, and indeed under a corresponding duty, to restore the parties, so far as may be, to the position they would have occupied but for the order or decree subsequently altered. The object of Section 144 CPC is not to confer any independent substantive right upon a litigant; rather, it provides a statutory mechanism for restoring the position disturbed by the operation of a judicial order or decree which has subsequently been varied or reversed. The provision requires the Court of first instance, upon an application by a party entitled to restitution, to make such consequential orders as may be necessary to place the parties, so far as possible, in the position they would have occupied but for the decree or the part thereof which has been varied or reversed. Subsection (2) further bars the institution of a separate suit for obtaining restitution or other relief which is obtainable by an application under subsection (1). The principle underlying this provision is that the jurisdiction of the Court does not stand exhausted merely because its earlier order has been acted upon or its consequences have been implemented. Where an order or decree is subsequently varied or reversed, the Court may grant restitution to undo its consequences and restore the parties, as far as practicable, to their original position. The precise nature and extent of restitution, however, must necessarily depend upon the nature of the order varied or reversed and the benefit received by the party against whom restitution is sought. In the present case, the delivery of possession to the decree-holder on 26.09.2025 is not, by itself, sufficient to establish that execution had lawfully attained finality in respect of Jabir Plates or that the respondents had been divested of their right to seek appropriate relief. The material question is whether the delivery of possession was consistent with the subsisting judicial directions and the qualification governing execution of the decree in respect of the disputed property.

13. Moreover, the record indicates that the judicial directions dated 20.05.2014 and 15.01.2025 required possession of Jabir Plates to remain subject to the final adjudication of the connected proceedings. The delivery of possession, therefore, could not be examined in isolation from those directions. If the execution proceedings had been carried forward in disregard of the subsisting restriction, the subsequent delivery of possession could not, merely by reason of its having taken place, extinguished the rights of the respondents or rendered their claim for appropriate restorative relief incompetent. It is also material that the application seeking suspension of execution had been dismissed by the learned Executing Court on 04.06.2025, whereas possession was delivered to the decree-holder subsequently, on 26.09.2025. The latter event could not retrospectively validate an order which was found legally unsustainable by this Court. Nor could the subsequent delivery of possession, by itself, defeat the effect of the judgment whereby the execution proceedings were restrained to the extent of Jabir Plates. The objection raised by Mr. Nazeer Ahmad, Advocate, therefore, proceeds on an erroneous assumption that delivery of possession, once effected, necessarily brings the controversy to an end. Such an approach overlooks the distinction between the physical implementation of an execution order and the legal sustainability of the proceedings through which possession was delivered. The former cannot, in every circumstance, foreclose examination of the latter, particularly where the execution was subject to an express judicial qualification. It is, however, clarified that the mere filing of an application under Section 144 CPC does not, by itself, establish an indefeasible entitlement to restoration of possession. The Court competent to entertain such application is required to determine whether the statutory conditions for restitution are fulfilled, whether the relief claimed falls within the scope of Section 144 CPC and whether the order or decree forming the basis of the alleged dispossession has been varied, reversed or otherwise displaced in a manner attracting the provision. The question of actual restitution, including its nature and extent, must be determined by the competent Court after examining the relevant record and affording the parties an opportunity of hearing. Nevertheless, the subsequent delivery of possession and the institution of proceedings for restitution do not furnish any ground for reviewing the judgment under consideration. Rather, these circumstances have to be examined in the light of the original decree, the subsisting judicial directions and the limited nature of the protection granted by this Court.

14. Mr. Nazeer Ahmad, Advocate, also referred to the application filed by the plaintiffs of the connected suit under Section 151 CPC, read with other enabling provisions of law, which was brought on record through C.M. No. 102-P/2026. However, the filing of such an application does not, in itself, establish any illegality in the judgment under review. The maintainability and merits of the subsequent application are matters to be determined by the competent Court in accordance with the applicable provisions of law. The present proceedings are confined to examining whether the judgment dated 11.09.2026 suffers from an error apparent on the face of the record or any other defect falling within the recognized parameters of review jurisdiction. The subsequent proceedings cannot be employed as a substitute for an appellate challenge to the findings already recorded by this Court.

15. It is now appropriate to consider the scope and extent of the review jurisdiction vested in this Court. No doubt, this Court possesses the power to review its own judgment under Section 114, read with Order XLVII CPC; however, such jurisdiction is not equivalent to appellate jurisdiction and cannot be exercised merely because a party remains dissatisfied with the conclusion reached by the Court. The power of review is confined to the grounds recognized by law, including discovery of new and important matter or evidence which, despite the exercise of due diligence, was not within the knowledge of the applicant or could not be produced at the relevant time, an error or mistake apparent on the face of the record, or any other sufficient reason falling within the scope of the governing principles. An error apparent on the face of the record must be self-evident and patent. It should be of such a nature that its existence can be established without undertaking an elaborate process of reasoning, reappraisal of evidence or reconsideration of legal questions already determined. A review petition cannot be used to secure a rehearing of the matter or to invite the Court to adopt a different view merely because another interpretation of the facts or law is also possible. The distinction between an erroneous decision and an error apparent on the face of the record must always be maintained. The former may furnish a ground for challenge before an appellate forum, where such remedy is available, but the latter alone can attract the corrective jurisdiction of review, subject to the other statutory grounds. The applicants have primarily sought reconsideration of the interpretation and applicability of Order XXI Rule 29 CPC, the status of the connected suit, the competence of the Executing Court to entertain the application and the effect of delivery of possession to the decree-holder. All these aspects were either directly considered or formed part of the controversy adjudicated through the judgment sought to be reviewed. The fact that the applicants seek to place a different interpretation upon the statutory provisions or attach a different legal consequence to the subsequent delivery of possession does not convert their objections into errors apparent on the face of the record.

16. It is equally significant that the alleged omission of Rule 29 from the applicable Code is founded upon a provincial amendment which, as discussed hereinabove, does not govern the present proceedings. Similarly, the judgments relied upon by learned counsel relate to a different statutory provision and do not displace the reasoning adopted in the judgment under review. The applicants have, therefore, failed to demonstrate any patent illegality, manifest mistake or jurisdictional defect warranting exercise of the review jurisdiction of this Court. This Court, while deciding the writ petition, examined the nature of the decree, the identity of the subject matter of the connected suit, the relevant judicial directions and the circumstances justifying a limited restraint upon execution. The judgment was confined to Jabir Plates and did not interfere with execution of the decree in respect of the remaining subject matter. The applicants have not been able to identify any error of such a fundamental or manifest nature as would justify recalling or modifying the said determination in exercise of the limited jurisdiction of review.

17. For what has been discussed above, it is evident that the objections raised by learned counsel for the applicants and Mr. Nazeer Ahmad, Advocate, do not disclose any ground falling within the recognized parameters of review jurisdiction. The judgment dated 11.09.2026 was rendered after consideration of the relevant factual and legal aspects of the controversy. The applicants, through the instant proceedings, have essentially sought a reconsideration of the merits of the decision, which is impermissible in review jurisdiction. Consequently, the instant review application, being devoid of merit, is hereby dismissed. No order as to costs.
Announced.
Asif Jan Sr. S.S.
JUDGE (SB) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Muhammad Naeem Anwar
